what-is-kafka.wrapped_text:
What Is Kafka?
Apache Kafka is a distributed event-streaming
platform for publishing, storing, and
processing streams of records. Producers
append events to durable, partitioned topics,
while consumers read those events
independently, making Kafka useful for
real-time data pipelines, event-driven
services, and streaming analytics.
what-is-kafka.wrapped_original_text:
What Is Kafka?
Apache Kafka is a distributed event-streaming platform for publishing, storing, and processing streams of records. Producers append events to durable, partitioned topics, while consumers read those events independently, making Kafka useful for real-time data pipelines, event-driven services, and streaming analytics.

how-kafka-works.wrapped_text:
How It Works
Kafka provides a durable, shared event log between
systems, so producers and consumers do not need to be
online at the same moment and multiple consumers can
independently use or replay the same data. In an IoT
setup, multiple sensors send measurements over local
device protocols to an edge device. A gateway application
running on that edge device collects, filters,
normalizes, batches, or aggregates the readings, then
uses a Kafka client to publish records to a topic such as
`sensor-readings`. Kafka brokers append each record to a
partition, retain it, and replicate it as configured. An
alerting service, time-series database sink, or data-lake
loader consumes the topic when ready. Kafka does not
automatically choose a destination: that work belongs to
a consumer application or Kafka Connect sink. The brokers
run centrally as a self-managed or managed cluster, while
the edge device and destination only need client or
connector software.

edge-device.wrapped_text:
Edge Device
A local computing device near the sensors, such as an
industrial PC, PLC, embedded controller, or gateway
appliance. It receives streams from multiple sensors
and provides compute, temporary buffering, local
processing, and network connectivity for sending
selected data upstream.

translates local device protocols, and can validate, normalize,
filter, batch, or aggregate readings before publishing them. It
is often the producer in an IoT setup.

Kafka Client
A language library or compatible interface used by an
application to authenticate with brokers and produce or
consume records. It handles Kafka's network protocol and
serializes outgoing keys and values or deserializes
incoming ones.

Kafka Server
An informal name for a machine or process
running Kafka. In normal Kafka terminology,
the server process that stores and serves data
is a broker.

kafka-broker.wrapped_text:
Kafka Broker
A Kafka server process that receives client requests
and stores topic partitions in append-only
log-segment files on its storage. Kafka does not
require an external database; brokers replicate
partition data with other brokers for fault
tolerance.

consumers read from it independently.

managed-kafka-service.wrapped_text:
Managed Kafka Service
A hosted offering that exposes Kafka-compatible cluster endpoints while the provider
operates the underlying service. Providers commonly handle compute, storage,
networking, broker and controller provisioning, security, monitoring, failed-node
replacement, patches, upgrades, scaling, partition rebalancing, and high availability.
You still design topics, keys, partitions, retention, schemas, producers, consumers, and
business processing; depending on the offering, the data plane may be open-source
Apache Kafka or a compatible managed engine.

sink.wrapped_text:
Sink
A consumer application or Kafka Connect sink connector that
reads a Kafka topic and writes records to an external
destination, such as a time-series database, data lake, or
alerting system.
sink.wrapped_original_text:
Sink

cluster.wrapped_text:
Cluster
A group of Kafka brokers working together as one service. A cluster spreads topic
partitions and their replicas across brokers for capacity and fault tolerance.
cluster.wrapped_original_text:
Cluster
A group of Kafka brokers working together as one service. A cluster spreads topic partitions and their replicas across brokers for capacity and fault tolerance.

event.wrapped_text:
Event
An event is the meaningful fact that happened, such as sensor `42` measuring `21.4°C`; a record is
Kafka's stored representation of that event, and message is an informal term often used for either.
A record carries a possibly null key, a value payload, a timestamp, and optional application-defined
headers; its topic is selected when produced, and Kafka assigns its partition and offset. The
producer serializes the key and value into bytes using JSON, Avro, Protocol Buffers, text, or
another agreed encoding, and the consumer deserializes those bytes. The key is application data
such as `sensor-42`, not inherently a hash, though the producer commonly hashes its serialized
bytes to choose a partition.

producer.wrapped_text:
Producer
An application role that publishes records to Kafka topics. In the IoT
example, the gateway is usually the producer and uses a Kafka client
library to send sensor readings.
producer.wrapped_original_text:

partition.wrapped_text:
Partition
A partition is one ordered, append-only shard
of a topic. Every record is written to one
partition and receives a sequential offset
there; multiple partitions distribute storage
and work across brokers, but ordering is
guaranteed only within a partition. When a key
is present, the producer normally hashes its
serialized bytes so the same key goes to the
same partition.
partition.wrapped_original_text:
Partition
A partition is one ordered, append-only shard of a topic. Every record is written to one partition and receives a sequential offset there; multiple partitions distribute storage and work across brokers, but ordering is guaranteed only within a partition. When a key is present, the producer normally hashes its serialized bytes so the same key goes to the same partition.

retention.wrapped_text:
Retention
Retention controls how long or how much of a
topic's log Kafka keeps, independently of
whether consumers have read it. Time- or
size-based retention removes old log segments,
while compaction can retain the latest record
for each key. Retention defines the replay
window; it is not a backup.
retention.wrapped_original_text:
Retention
Retention controls how long or how much of a topic's log Kafka keeps, independently of whether consumers have read it. Time- or size-based retention removes old log segments, while compaction can retain the latest record for each key. Retention defines the replay window; it is not a backup.

replication.wrapped_text:
Replication
Replication keeps copies of each partition on
different brokers. With replication factor
`3`, one leader serves the partition while two
followers copy it and an in-sync follower can
take over after failure. Replication improves
availability and durability, but it multiplies
storage and does not replace backup or extend
retention.

consumer.wrapped_text:
Consumer
An application role that reads records from topic partitions and processes
them. Reading does not delete records; a consumer tracks offsets so it can
continue from its last position or intentionally replay earlier data.

client-serializes-sends.wrapped_text:
Client Serializes & Sends
The client serializes the key and value into bytes,
chooses a partition—normally using the key—and finds
its leader through cluster metadata. It reuses a
persistent TCP connection, or opens one when needed,
and sends a binary Kafka produce request; DNS, IP
routing, optional TLS and authentication, packet
transport, retries, and acknowledgements are handled
underneath.

runtime-model.wrapped_text:
Runtime Model
Kafka is not one infinite loop searching external systems for
messages. It is a collection of long-running broker server
processes and client applications communicating over
persistent TCP connections: producers push records to
brokers, consumers pull records from brokers, and brokers
store the records between them.

Runtime Model

producer-application.wrapped_text:
Producer Application
In the IoT example, the gateway application typically runs a loop that
waits for sensor readings. When data arrives, it builds a record and
asks its Kafka client to serialize, batch, and push the record to a
broker; Kafka itself does not inspect the sensors.

broker-process.wrapped_text:
Broker Process
A broker is a long-running Kafka server
process, commonly run as an operating-system
service, container, or Kubernetes workload. At
startup it loads its partition logs, joins the
cluster, opens configured TCP
listeners—commonly on port `9092`—and waits
efficiently for client and broker requests. A
managed Kafka provider runs these broker
processes for you.

broker-request-handling.wrapped_text:
Request Handling
Network I/O and request-handler loops wait on sockets rather than
repeatedly scanning for data. A produce request is validated and
appended to a partition log; a fetch request asks for records after an
offset and may be held briefly until data arrives, avoiding a wasteful
busy loop.

broker-background-work.wrapped_text:
Background Work
Kafka continuously performs internal maintenance alongside client
requests. Followers fetch partition updates from leaders, retention
removes expired log segments, compaction and log maintenance
manage storage, and cluster coordination tracks metadata and broker
leadership.
broker-background-work.wrapped_original_text:

consumer-application.wrapped_text:
Consumer Application
A consumer application typically runs a poll
loop that asks Kafka for records after its
current partition offsets. Kafka may hold an
empty fetch request open briefly, then returns
new records or a timeout; the consumer
deserializes and processes the results. Kafka
does not push records to the destination, and
reading them does not delete them.

producer-bootstrap-metadata.wrapped_text:
Bootstrap & Metadata
The client starts with one or more bootstrap addresses such as `kafka-
1.example.com:9092`. It resolves a hostname to an IP address, opens a TCP
connection, and requests cluster metadata to learn which brokers exist and
which broker leads each topic partition; the bootstrap broker is an entry point,
not a permanent proxy.

producer-persistent-connections.wrapped_text:
Persistent Connections
The client maintains and reuses TCP connections to the brokers it needs
instead of opening a new connection for every record. Connections may
cross a private network, VPN, or the internet and commonly use TLS
encryption plus authentication; the client handles reconnecting and retrying
when connections fail.

producer-produce-request.wrapped_text:
Produce Request
Calling `producer.send(record)` makes the client serialize and batch records
into Kafka's binary produce-request format, then send the bytes through a
TCP connection to the partition's leader broker. TCP divides the request
into IP packets for network transport, and the broker returns an
acknowledgement according to the producer's configuration.
